query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Grain refining the FeNiCrCoCu coating via a post-deposition annealing treatment increases the density of grain boundaries, which in turn promotes a more continuous, protective oxide layer during high‐temperature sliding, thereby reducing adhesive wear and moderating microscopic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating with a typical multi-phase microstructure and coarse grains on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-deposition annealing treatment to refine the grain size and increase the grain boundary density.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding tests conducted at temperatures between 300°C and 600°C under defined normal loads and sliding speeds.
generation.structural_mediator: The increased grain boundary density leads to accelerated local oxidation at the boundaries, forming a continuous and adherent thin oxide layer across the coating.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature sliding conditions, the refined microstructure facilitates rapid oxidation at the grain boundaries, resulting in a thin, stable oxide layer that acts as a lubricative barrier. This barrier minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact (limiting adhesive wear) and also influences dislocation motion, moderating plastic deformation and promoting dynamic recrystallization in the subsurface layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as-deposited coating, the annealed, grain-refined coating will show significantly lower wear rates and modified microscopic deformation patterns (e.g., less adhesive wear and more controlled plastic deformation) due to the formation of a robust oxide layer during high-temperature sliding.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu coating as deposited without additional annealing treatment.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under sliding conditions at 300–600°C with controlled normal loads and sliding speeds; outcomes outside this temperature regime or under substantially different mechanical loading are not predicted by this mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence supports the role of grain size in promoting beneficial oxide layer formation and wear resistance, the exact contributions of dynamic recrystallization and dislocation dynamics during high-temperature sliding remain partially uncertain and may require further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coated samples: one in the as-deposited state and another subjected to a controlled annealing treatment designed to refine the grain structure. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding tests (300–600°C) under the same normal loads and sliding speeds. Use microscopic surface characterization (such as SEM and TEM) to analyze the continuity and thickness of the oxide layer, alongside quantitative measurements of wear rate and friction coefficient.
measurements: Grain size distribution and grain boundary density (via TEM/SEM)
Continuity and thickness of the oxide layer (via surface analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed, grain-refined samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and do not show evidence of a more continuous, protective oxide layer and modified microscopic deformation patterns compared to the as-deposited baseline under high-temperature sliding conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

AbstractThe effect and mechanism of grain sizes on the tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) were studied by friction experiments and wear morphology analysis. Under normal low load and low sliding speed, the primary wear mechanism of the HEA samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the samples are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG. With the increase of normal load and sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the HEA samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation. The oxide layer of CG sample has many cracks, and the worn surface also has plastic deformation, which leads to the increase of friction coefficient and specific wear rate and the decrease of wear resistance. Therefore, the fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.Keywords: high entropy alloy, grain size, tribological behavior, wear mechanism

In the present study, the tribological properties of different grain sizes CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were systematically analyzed based on sliding experiments and worn surface morphology characterization under different sliding speeds and normal loads. The results can be summarized as follows: Under the normal low load and low sliding speed, the main wear mechanism of FG and CG samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. However, the material of CG is easy to soften under the action of friction heat during high sliding speed, and the oxide layer formed is easy to fracture. Under the normal high load, the wear mechanisms of FG and CG samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation with the increase of sliding speed. The oxidation layer formed on CG sample has many cracks, and the wear surface of CG sample also has plastic deformation, resulting in an increase in friction coefficient and specific wear rate and a decrease in wear resistance. Therefore, under high load and low load, FG sample has good wear resistance due to its high surface strength.

frame.system: A FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy applied as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, where the initial state comprises its typical multi-phase microstructure and grain architecture under ambient processing conditions before any sliding tests.
frame.goal: To elucidate the mechanistic link between controlled microstructural/chemical changes in the coating and the resulting overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation behavior during high-temperature sliding.
frame.limitation: There is currently no single, testable mechanistic hypothesis that connects a controlled change in the coating (e.g., modifying grain size, phase fraction, or oxidation propensity) directly with directional variations in wear and deformation under high-temperature sliding regimes.
root_cause_cues: controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition
constraints: Hypothesis must be single and testable
It requires a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition
It must predict directional changes in both wear and microscopic deformation
It must clearly specify the high-temperature sliding regime where these predictions are valid
It should identify supporting prior evidence and set a falsifiable criterion (i.e., a result that would reject the hypothesis)
frame.regime: High-temperature sliding conditions (e.g., at operating temperatures roughly between 300°C and 600°C under a defined normal load and sliding speed)
prior_attempts: Previous investigations have separately considered mechanisms such as oxidation-induced wear reduction, dynamic recrystallization at elevated temperatures, and grain-boundary mediated deformation in similar alloys. However, these studies did not integrate these aspects into a unified, controlled hypothesis with clear directional predictions linking specific microstructural modifications to wear and deformation outcomes.

decision.trend: Early work in high-entropy alloys has focused on manipulating microstructure via processing routes such as cold rolling, mechanical alloying, laser cladding, and even ultrasonic assistance to affect wear resistance and deformation behavior. Initial studies examined phenomena like dislocation mechanisms and grain boundary‐dominated responses (e.g., inverse Hall-Petch behavior), albeit largely at room temperature or in inert environments. More recent investigations have begun to probe temperature-dependent deformation (e.g., in refractory HEAs) and phase coupling effects under wear, suggesting that microstructural features—especially grain size and the nature of phase boundaries—play a critical role. However, these studies treated mechanisms such as oxidation-induced wear improvement, dynamic recrystallization, and grain boundary-mediated deformation separately, leaving a unified, controlled hypothesis for high-temperature sliding in coatings unaddressed.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved how a deliberately controlled microstructural change—specifically one that alters the density and behavior of grain boundaries—can be directly linked to both directional changes in overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation under high-temperature sliding conditions. In particular, the interplay between enhanced grain boundary oxidation (potentially forming a protective, lubricious layer) and in situ dynamic recrystallization during sliding has not been unified into a single testable mechanistic hypothesis.
decision.lever: Apply a controlled post-deposition heat treatment (annealing) to refine the grain size of the FeNiCrCoCu coating, thereby increasing grain boundary density. Then, perform sliding wear tests at high temperatures (300–600°C) while systematically varying the annealing conditions (temperature/time) to modulate grain boundary oxidation characteristics.
decision.why: This next step follows the trend of linking microstructural control to mechanical performance by directly testing whether controlled grain refinement enhances the formation of a continuous, thin oxide layer at grain boundaries. Such a layer could act as a self-adjusting, protective mechanism that both reduces wear and alters microscopic deformation, thereby unifying prior separate observations (oxidation effects, grain boundary deformation, and dynamic recrystallization) into a single, mechanistically testable hypothesis.
